column4: The section pairs niʿma as blessing with h-d-y as guidance. This ayah portrays Abraham as grateful for God's favors and then guided to a straight path, bringing those two roots together in one account of divine favor and human response.

The section's gift root ʿaṭā becomes an offering in its reciprocal reading. This ayah contributes the person who gives and is mindful; 92:7 completes the sequence by promising that God will ease that person's way, reversing the section's order of divine giving followed by human response.

The section reads sacrifice as a return for what God has given. This ayah states a specific reciprocal movement: what people spend is replaced by God, the best provider. It presents that giving relation in the opposite direction, without naming sacrifice.

This ayah joins honoring Allah's sacred ordinances to livestock made lawful under stated limits. It gives the section's sacred animal a frame of sanctuary law before the surrounding passage describes the rites and sacrificial animals.

The section's dictionary note ties the ḍuḥā root to the Eid offering; here the same forenoon word marks a time when divine punishment may reach a town at play. This is only a contrast in the time's valence, since the ayah itself describes no sacrifice.

The section's secondary dictionary sense says hady can mean camels; this ayah names camels among livestock pairs. That anchors the animal sense only: the ayah itself debates animal restrictions and does not describe a Hady offering.
